title: Creating Sashimi-Style Plots with `spliceTerrain`
text: Several established tools support related visualisation tasks: Gviz provides genomic tracks, including BAM-backed coverage sashimi plots (Hahne Ivanek 2016). ggbio provides genomic visualisation based ggplot2, support Bioconductor objects transcript-based splice summaries (Yin et al. 2012). SpliceWiz provides coverage sashimi plots within alternative-splicing analysis workflow. event-normalised coverage plots offer alternative view splicing differences, summarising replicates condition rather relying individual-sample sashimi plots (Wong et al. 2024). ggsashimi provides command-line sashimi plotting workflow sample overlays aggregation (Garrido-Martín et al. 2018). spliceTerrain focuses sample-resolved sashimi plots within R/Bioconductor workflows. particularly useful regions annotations already represented genomic objects plots need iterative refinement. combines: Editable genomic summaries: inspect modify coverage, junctions, settings returned context, replot without importing BAM files . Coverage-aware compression: preserve selected blocks defined coverage, annotation, junction anchors shortening gaps. Coverage retained filtering can preserve regions within annotated introns original width. Fragment-level support: count overlapping mates per covered base per distinct junction, retaining mapped singletons. Stable local junction fractions: calculate usage pre-display junction reference, hiding arcs change remaining percentages. Integrated sample normalisation: apply supplied library sizes optional normalisation factors consistently coverage junction support, retaining raw fragment counts filtering. choices offer specific contrasts existing workflows. compression enabled, ggsashimi uses junction-derived, length-dependent shrinking, whereas spliceTerrain also uses retained coverage annotation define preserved blocks. default, Gviz ggsashimi count support read level, mates can contribute coverage junction counts. contrast, spliceTerrain uses fragment-level counts. spliceTerrain displays transcript annotation alongside observed junction support without assigning support transcript models. complements transcript-model-based summaries provided ggbio’s plotSpliceSum(). spliceTerrain exposes sample normalisation dedicated arguments. Gviz supports custom transformations can implement similar scaling, whereas ggsashimi command-line interface equivalent library-size normalisation option. Versions compared: Gviz 1.57.4, ggbio 1.61.0, SpliceWiz 1.15.0, ggsashimi 1.1.5.

text: Consider cassette exon upstream downstream exon. simplified example, 50 inclusion fragments support inclusion junctions, 50 skipping fragments support direct skipping junction. range selecting three junctions gives following junction-usage labels: denominator 150 units junction support, label 33.3%. 100 fragments constructed example, known exon inclusion fraction 50%: inclusion fragment supports two junctions. Ranges remain useful inspecting broader patterns, combined junction fractions interpreted general event-level percent spliced (PSI) transcript-isoform proportions.
code: cassette <- data.frame(     Junction = c("Upstream inclusion", "Downstream inclusion", "Skipping"),     Fragments = c(50L, 50L, 50L) ) cassette[["Junction usage (%)"]] <- round(     100 * cassette$Fragments / sum(cassette$Fragments), 1 ) pander(cassette)

Scripts AI agents working within R session can inspect coverage junction summaries, check values underlying plotted labels, modify annotations plotting settings redrawing figure. provides access data behind visualisation without requiring values inferred plot image. context can passed back ctx argument redraw plot without re-importing BAM files recalculating coverage junctions. example, annotation can used retain coverage overlapping annotated exons junctions exactly match annotated introns.  annotation_match field records whether junction exactly matches intron implied supplied annotation. code: if (   requireNamespace("RNAseqData.HNRNPC.bam.chr14", quietly = TRUE) &&   requireNamespace("EnsDb.Hsapiens.v75", quietly = TRUE) &&   requireNamespace("AnnotationFilter", quietly = TRUE) &&   requireNamespace("ensembldb", quietly = TRUE) ) {   bams <- RNAseqData.HNRNPC.bam.chr14::RNAseqData.HNRNPC.bam.chr14_BAMFILES   bams <- bams[c(7, 1)]   names(bams) <- c("HNRNPC knockdown", "Control")   region <- "chr14:70,233,810-70,238,690"    annotation <- ensembldb::exonsBy(     EnsDb.Hsapiens.v75::EnsDb.Hsapiens.v75,     by = "tx",     filter = AnnotationFilter::GeneIdFilter("ENSG00000100650")   )   annotation <- annotation[1:3]   ensembldb::seqlevelsStyle(annotation) <- "ucsc"    spliceTerrain(bam = bams, region = region)    spliceTerrain(     bam = bams,     region = region,     lib_size = c(40e6, 55e6),     norm_factors = c(0.95, 1.08),     common_y = TRUE   )    spliceTerrain(     bam = bams,     region = region,     annotation = annotation,     anno_fill_by = "group",     anno_fill_colours = c(         ENST00000553369 = "#66C2A5",         ENST00000394366 = "#8DA0CB",         ENST00000451983 = "#FC8D62"     ),     anno_label_by = "exon_rank",     anno_label_colour = "black",     junction_usage = "chr14:70234854-70234854",     highlight = "chr14:70233810-70234097",     arc_height = 2,     arc_side = "above",     arc_scale = TRUE,     common_y = TRUE,     colours = c("darkblue", "darkred"),     highlight_colour = scales::alpha("gold", 0.25),     anno_label_size = 2,     panel_heights = c(2, 2, 1)   )    ctx <- spliceTerrain(     bam = bams,     region = region,     annotation = annotation,     min_junction_reads = 1,     panel_heights = c(2, 2, 1),     return_ctx = TRUE   )   ctx$juncs <- ctx$juncs[ctx$juncs$coverage >= 20]   spliceTerrain(ctx = ctx) }
